chief_complaint: difficulty swallowing both food and liquids for 9 months
hpi_details: 9-month worsening dysphagia equally affecting solid food and liquids from the onset. Experiences sensation of food sticking in the lower chest, frequent regurgitation of bland, undigested food at night, and retrosternal chest tightness. Lost 4kg over 6 months due to fear of eating. Denies heartburn or acid taste.
ideas: thinks her throat muscles have stopped working properly
concerns: afraid she might choke to death while sleeping due to regurgitation
expectations: wants a procedure to open up her esophagus so she can drink fluids normally
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks wine socially, teacher, sleeps propped up on three pillows

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Achalasia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Referral for high-resolution manometry and diagnostic gastroscopy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: difficulty swallowing both food and liquids for 9 months

Key HPI features: 9-month worsening dysphagia equally affecting solid food and liquids from the onset. Experiences sensation of food sticking in the lower chest, frequent regurgitation of bland, undigested food at night, and retrosternal chest tightness. Lost 4kg over 6 months due to fear of eating. Denies heartburn or acid taste.

Objective/Exam findings: General exam for nutrition status. OGD (gastroscopy) to exclude mechanical obstruction or pseudoachalasia (malignancy at gastro-oesophageal junction). High-resolution oesophageal manometry (gold standard showing aperistalsis and failure of LES relaxation). Barium swallow ('bird-beak' appearance).
Relevant background/PMH: hypothyroidism, mild allergic rhinitis
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Achalasia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastric cardia adenocarcinoma (pseudoachalasia) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Choking or aspiration risk from nighttime regurgitation.
management_principles: Referral for high-resolution manometry and diagnostic gastroscopy
Discuss therapeutic options: pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, or Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM)
Advise upright posture for 2 hours after meals and sleeping with head elevated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 48F presents with 9-month progressive dysphagia to solids AND liquids from onset, regurgitation of undigested food, retrosternal fullness, and 4kg weight loss.
reference_soap.objective: General exam for nutrition status. OGD (gastroscopy) to exclude mechanical obstruction or pseudoachalasia (malignancy at gastro-oesophageal junction). High-resolution oesophageal manometry (gold standard showing aperistalsis and failure of LES relaxation). Barium swallow ('bird-beak' appearance).
reference_soap.assessment: Achalasia cardiae. DDx: pseudoachalasia secondary to gastric cardia adenocarcinoma, diffuse oesophageal spasm, peptic stricture, eosinophilic oesophagitis.
reference_soap.plan: Referral for high-resolution manometry and diagnostic gastroscopy. Discuss therapeutic options: pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, or Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM). Advise upright posture for 2 hours after meals and sleeping with head elevated.

learning_objectives: Differentiate motility dysphagia (solids and liquids simultaneously) from mechanical stricture (solids progressing to liquids)
Identify nocturnal regurgitation and aspiration risk factors in esophageal outflow obstruction
Outline the diagnostic step-up approach: endoscopy, barium contrast, and manometry
Discuss definitive interventions for lower esophageal sphincter hypertonicity clearly

teaching.one_liner: The lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and the oesophagus loses its normal squeezing motion, so both solids and liquids get stuck and come back up.
red_flags: Choking or aspiration risk from nighttime regurgitation

must_ask.say: Does it feel like both solid food and liquids get stuck, right from the start?
Do you ever bring up food that looks undigested, especially at night?
Where do you feel the tightness — is it behind your breastbone?

must_ask.objective: Weight loss and fear of eating
must_ask.say: Have you lost weight because you're avoiding food out of fear of it sticking?
Why do you sleep propped up on pillows — is it to stop the regurgitation?
Do you get any heartburn or acid taste, or is it just the food sticking?

history.answer: I've been having a lot of trouble swallowing both food and liquids for about nine months now.
It started about nine months ago and has steadily gotten worse over time.
I can start the swallow just fine, but a few seconds later it feels stuck right behind the lower part of my breastbone.
Right from the very beginning, both solid food and liquids like water have been getting stuck equally.
Yes, food often gets stuck and won't go down. Drinking water doesn't help at all and usually just makes it feel fuller and more stuck.
Frequently at night, undigested food that tastes completely bland comes back up into my mouth. There is no sour or acidic taste to it.
I sleep propped up on three pillows because food comes up when I lie flat, and I'm terrified I might choke to death in my sleep.
I don't choke or cough immediately when I swallow, but I wake up coughing at night when food comes back up. I have never had pneumonia.
I get a tight, heavy fullness right behind my breastbone, especially after I try to eat.
No, it doesn't hurt when I swallow; it just feels like it's jammed and cannot pass through.
No, I have never had heartburn, burning in my chest, or an acid taste in my mouth.
I have lost about four kilograms over the past six months, mostly because I'm afraid to eat since everything gets stuck.
No, I haven't thrown up any blood, my stools look normal brown, and I haven't been told I'm anemic.
No, my voice hasn't changed, and I don't have any hoarseness.
No slurred speech, no facial drooping, no arm or leg weakness, and no drooping eyelids or double vision.
I have mild allergic rhinitis with seasonal sneezing, but I don't have asthma, eczema, or known food allergies.
No, I always drink plenty of water when I take my thyroid pill in the morning, and I'm not on any immunosuppressants.
No, my fingers don't turn white or blue in the cold, and my skin hasn't become tight or thick anywhere.
No, I haven't noticed any lumps or swelling in my neck.
Honestly, I feel like the muscles in my throat or food pipe have completely stopped working properly.
I'm really terrified that I might choke and suffocate in my sleep from food coming back up into my throat.
I'm hoping you can perform a procedure or stretch open my esophagus so I can swallow liquids and food normally again.
I have hypothyroidism and mild allergic rhinitis. I have no history of high blood pressure or diabetes.
I haven't had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I take levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily every morning for my thyroid. I don't take any other prescriptions or over-the-counter supplements.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and I haven't had much lately because of the swallowing issue.
I work as an elementary school teacher and live at home with my husband and two teenage children.
There is no family history of esophageal cancer, stomach cancer, or gastrointestinal diseases.
My last period was about two weeks ago. My cycles are regular every 28 days, my husband had a vasectomy, and there is no chance I'm pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and well-appearing, slightly thin but well-hydrated, with no acute respiratory or physical distress.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink without white plaques, ulcers, or dental decay; uvula elevates symmetrically in the midline.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules or bruit.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact; normal palate elevation, clear articulation without dysarthria, and no ptosis or facial weakness.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without crackles, rhonchi, or wheezing.
Regular rhythm and rate with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with normal active bowel sounds.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout without guarding; no palpable epigastric mass or organomegaly.
No signs of skin thickening, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, or peripheral edema.
